question: What does matching the hatch mean in fly fishing?
answer: Matching the hatch means selecting an artificial fly that closely imitates the color, size, shape, and behavior of the natural insects trout are actively feeding on at a specific moment. When a hatch is occurring trout become selective — keying on one stage of one insect and refusing everything else. The challenge is identifying not just the species but the stage: nymph, emerger, winged adult, or spent spinner. Each requires a different fly and often a different presentation.

question: How do I know what insects are hatching on the water?
answer: Four methods — in order of reliability. First, observe rise forms: a splashy rise usually indicates caddis pupa; a slow sip indicates spent spinners or emergers in the film; a head-and-tail rise indicates duns. Second, look at the water surface for drifting insects. Third, check streamside vegetation and the air for flying adults. Fourth, use a stomach pump on a caught fish to see exactly what it has been eating — the most definitive method available.

question: Is matching the hatch always necessary for catching trout?
answer: No — and it is often overrated. Drift matters more than pattern in the vast majority of fishing situations. A perfectly matched fly with micro drag will be refused. An attractor pattern with a perfect drag-free drift will be eaten. Attractor patterns with hot spots, colored triggers, and rubber legs consistently outperform precise imitations on the wild streams of the Smoky Mountains — which is why Mac Brown's hatch chart recommends attractor elements even on imitative patterns.

question: What are the most important hatches to match in the Smoky Mountains?
answer: Caddisflies are the most abundant insect family in the region — over 330 species identified in the surrounding watershed. Match caddis in larval, pupal, and adult forms year-round. Spring brings Quill Gordons, Blue Quills, and Hendricksons. Fall is defined by the October Caddis. Winter produces midge and BWO hatches on mild overcast days. Water temperature is the most reliable predictor of hatch activity — the full hatch chart for Western North Carolina is available at macbrownflyfish.com.

question: What is a stomach pump and should I use one?
answer: A stomach pump is a small rubber bulb with a soft tube used to extract stomach contents from a live trout without harming it — allowing the angler to see exactly what the fish has been eating. Used correctly and carefully it is the most definitive hatch-matching tool available. Mac Brown collected over 14,000 stomach samples from wild regional trout over 40 years to build the Bryson City Area Hatch Chart — the most comprehensive hatch data available for Western North Carolina.
